query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 1 atomic percent aluminum during casting of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr promotes the selective formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature air exposure, which will improve the alloy's oxygen resistance without degrading its intrinsic room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, but with inadequate oxygen resistance resulting in pesting during high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (~1 at.%) aluminum addition into the alloy during the casting process.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at approximately 800 °C for up to 5 hours, with subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy's surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the added Al selectively oxidizes to form a protective alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen. This barrier slows down further oxidation (pesting) of the refractory elements in the alloy without significantly altering the bulk microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Al-doped variant will show a markedly reduced oxidation rate (evidenced by lower weight gain and minimal scale spallation) while retaining similar ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (approximately 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure, despite its favorable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions of high-temperature air exposure (around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours) and mechanical testing conditions relevant to high-temperature applications (e.g., tensile tests at 1000 °C with strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). Effects outside these temperature and time windows remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the long-term stability of the alumina scale over extended exposures beyond 5 hours or potential subtle impacts on microstructural evolution that might affect mechanical properties at more extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast samples: (1) the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and (2) the same alloy with an added ~1 at.% Al. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under no applied mechanical load. After exposure, perform surface characterization using SEM/EDS and XRD to assess the continuity and composition of the oxide scale. Additionally, conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C (with strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation rates
SEM/EDS and XRD analyses to verify the formation and integrity of an alumina (Al2O3) scale
Tensile tests at room temperature and high temperature (1000 °C) to evaluate ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not form a continuous, adherent alumina scale (or if the scale spalls or is ineffective), shows similar or increased oxidation rates (as measured by weight gain and surface degradation) compared to the baseline, or if its mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) degrade significantly relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Isothermal oxidation experiments allow one to determine the rate of growth of an oxide scale. This is a measure of the performance of an alloy but it is at best a poor yardstick. Oxidation resistance does not depend only on the rate at which an oxide scale thickens but must also consider the ability of the scale to resist the thermally induced stresses associated with cyclic behaviour. We plan to evaluate the latter for the alloy Nb1.3Si2.4Ti2.4Al3.5Hf0.4, as well as its CTE and mechanical properties. The microstructures and isothermal oxidation of other alumina scale forming alloys of the same alloy system will be discussed in future publication.

The oxides of Hf, Nb and Ti do not form as compact layer during oxidation and therefore permit gaseous transport of oxygen to the substrate. The design and selection of new alloys of the Nb-Ti-Si-Al-Hf system had as objects to eliminate the intermixed Al2O3/TiO2 scale, to decrease the growth of niobates [] and to form stable αAl2O3 scale. The design and selection of the two alloys that are the subject of this paper was guided by our understanding of the alloying behaviour of Nb5Si3 and how it affects its properties [], the alloy design methodology NICE [], the research that was reported in [], the Wagner–Hauffe (W-H) rule [,,,] and Wagner’s oxidation theory [].

The formation of rod-like oxides of θAl2O3 at phase boundaries cannot be discarded []. Hf additions have been shown to enhance the scale adhesion in alumina forming alloys, for example see [,,,,,,]. In the alloy OHC3 there was no oxide buckling. This was attributed to the addition of Hf that acted as reactive element and promoted the formation of Hf-rich particles at the oxide grain boundaries. Chromium addition in Al-rich Nb-Al alloys would be expected to reduce oxygen solubility and diffusivity (see Section 2.2) and enhance the oxidation resistance of Nb-Cr-Al alloys by increasing the Al activity []. The oxygen solubility and diffusivity in the alloy at 800 °C was not reduced to a level low enough to prevent internal oxidation. frame.system: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy that currently has acceptable room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature strength but suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) during high-temperature air exposure.
frame.goal: Improve the oxygen resistance (oxidation behavior) at high temperatures without compromising the beneficial mechanical properties at room and high temperatures.
frame.limitation: Inadequate oxygen resistance for practical high-temperature applications, despite mechanical properties being within useful ranges.
root_cause_cues: earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy
related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
Must preserve the useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance
The intervention should be applicable in a cast state
frame.regime: Target application conditions are high temperature (around 800 °C to 1000 °C) in air (oxidizing atmosphere) with exposure durations on the order of 5 hours, and mechanical loading conditions corresponding to reported strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) in tensile testing.
prior_attempts: Earlier work on a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy used an oxidation-protection strategy to prevent pesting at 800 °C for 5 hours, but this did not directly translate to the equiatomic composition.
Studies on other refractory alloys attempted oxidation protection but did not evaluate the equiatomic composition, leaving an open question for this specific alloy.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis aims to explain and demonstrate that a minor compositional modification (a single intervention) can lead to the formation of a protective oxide scale that inhibits oxygen diffusion without degrading the alloy’s mechanical properties.
frame.hypothesis_intervention: Introduce a small addition (e.g., ~1 at.% or another minimal amount) of a reactive element such as aluminum (Al) into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy during casting. The expectation is that during high-temperature exposure, Al will selectively oxidize to form a continuous, slow-growing, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface, thereby enhancing oxygen resistance.
frame.mechanism: The Al addition lowers the oxygen affinity of the surface by forming an Al2O3 layer that acts as a diffusion barrier, protecting the underlying refractory elements from rapid oxidation (pesting), while the low volume fraction prevents significant changes to the base alloy microstructure and thus preserves the room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
frame.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-doped alloy should exhibit markedly reduced oxidation rates (minimal weight gain and surface scale spallation) when exposed to air at temperatures around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours, while maintaining similar tensile ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (approximately 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under specified strain rates).
frame.controlled_experiment: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) baseline equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr and (2) equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a minor (~1 at.%) Al addition. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under no applied load to simulate environmental exposure. Then, conduct comparative analyses of surface oxide scales (via SEM/EDS and XRD) and measure weight gain. Additionally, perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature (e.g., 1000 °C at 10−4–10−2 s−1) to verify that mechanical performance remains intact.
frame.falsification_criteria: If the Al-doped samples do not develop a continuous, protective alumina scale (or if the scale spalls off) and exhibit similar or worsened oxidation behavior (e.g., comparable weight gain, pesting, or surface degradation) compared to the untreated alloy, or if the slight composition change degrades the mechanical properties beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

families.principle: Altering the alloy’s chemistry to modify the thermodynamics and kinetics of oxidation, specifically by enabling selective oxidation of an added element (e.g., Al) to form a protective, adherent alumina scale that slows oxygen ingress.

hypothesis intervention: add a minor (~1 at.%) reactive element such as Al to form a protective oxide
cues_against: none directly; the design emphasizes preservation of the cast state and mechanical properties, which requires only a minor compositional tweak
families.best_lever: Introduce ~1 at.% Al during casting so that during high-temperature exposure, an adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale forms, thereby improving oxygen resistance without altering the bulk mechanical properties.

families.principle: Using controlled heat treatments to modify the surface oxide layer’s formation or the underlying microstructure to improve oxidation resistance through enhanced diffusion barriers.
cues_for: performance is evaluated at high temperatures (800 °C to 1000 °C), where thermal treatments might alter oxidation behavior
cues_against: must preserve the as-cast mechanical properties, and applying additional thermal treatments may alter the microstructure undesirably
prior studies on oxidation protection in similar alloys did not focus on post-cast heat treatments for this composition
families.best_lever: A brief post-casting anneal in a controlled, low-oxygen atmosphere to pre-form a protective oxide may help, though it risks altering the optimized microstructure.

families.principle: Engineering the surface via coatings or treatments to create a barrier to oxygen diffusion. This includes applying or inducing a protective scale without altering the bulk alloy.
cues_for: the goal is improved oxygen resistance, which is directly linked to surface behavior
earlier oxidation‐protection research on related alloys has sometimes leveraged surface scale formation
cues_against: the intervention must be a single modification applicable in the cast state and maintain bulk mechanical properties; post-production coatings or processes risk decoupling the surface from the bulk
prior attempts did not focus on adding external layers for this exact composition
families.best_lever: Employ a brief in-situ surface pre-oxidation step to form a continuous protective alumina layer; however, this is less appealing than a compositional approach that integrates the protection inherently during casting.

families.principle: Modifying the casting or synthesis conditions to control impurities, defect density, or oxidation kinetics through adjusted cooling rates or atmosphere, potentially influencing the formation of protective surface scales.
cues_for: cast state (the alloy is produced by casting)
cues_against: constraint that the intervention must be a single change that preserves the as-cast mechanical properties
earlier work focused on composition rather than processing changes
families.best_lever: Optimize the casting atmosphere (e.g., inert gas shielding) to minimize oxygen contamination during casting, though this is less promising given the focus on a chemical barrier approach.

families.principle: Tailoring the internal microstructural features (such as grain size, phase distribution, or the dispersion of oxide particles) to intrinsically improve oxidation resistance by hindering oxygen diffusion pathways.
cues_for: the need to preserve mechanical properties suggests that any microstructural modifications must be subtle
cues_against: the alloy is in a cast state and major alterations to the microstructure through heat treatments or mechanical working are not desirable
earlier approaches and the hypothesis favor a compositional tweak rather than microstructural modifications
families.best_lever: Refining the grain structure during solidification might slightly improve oxidation behavior, but it is less promising compared to directly forming a protective oxide via compositional changes.
